summary:
AstroMed is a health check-in tool for astronauts. You use it in three steps:

Check your vitals. Scan your face with the camera for pulse and breathing, and type in readings from your devices, such as blood pressure and sleep. The system tells you whether each one is normal, worth watching, or needs action.
Find out what’s wrong. If something hurts, click the spot on the 3D body, describe it by typing or speaking, and do one quick test. You get likely causes, what to do now, and which supplies to use.
Get help. Vela, the voice assistant, explains results aloud and you can talk to her. Anything serious is packed into a brief for the doctors on Earth.

The goal is to let crew handle health problems themselves when Earth is too far away to answer quickly.
details:
AstroMed: project details

What it does and how it works

AstroMed is a health assistant for astronauts, who often can’t get quick medical help from Earth. It has three parts.

  • Daily baseline. A webcam scan reads pulse, breathing and heart-rhythm variation from tiny colour changes in the face (remote photoplethysmography). Crew also enter readings from their devices: blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, oxygen, sleep and cabin CO₂. Each reading is rated Nominal, Monitor or Action against ranges adjusted for where the crew member is: orbital station, deep-space transit, lunar surface or planetary base. It also flags slow drifts across the past week.
  • Symptom detective. The astronaut taps a spot on a 3D body, viewable as skin, organs or bones. They describe the symptom by typing or speaking, then run one short test, such as a vision grid, a reflex test or a breathing check. They can also upload a photo for AI review. The result is a ranked list of likely causes, step-by-step care, and which supply pouch to use.
  • Vela, the voice assistant. She reads results aloud and can hold a spoken conversation, with the crew member’s current readings and location as context.

Anything yellow or red is packed into a brief for the flight surgeons. It shows the radio delay to Earth and can be saved as a PDF or JSON file. A what-if simulator lets presenters trigger a solar particle event, a CO₂ spike or a fluid shift and watch the whole system react.

Benefits

  • Care starts on board instead of waiting 13 to 20 minutes or more for a reply.
  • Everything is in plain language, with one clear next step.
  • It catches gradual problems that a single day of readings would hide.
  • The camera scan needs no extra sensors, and voice works when hands are busy.

Intended impact

To help crew understand and manage common health issues themselves on long missions. It escalates to a crewmate or the ground only when needed, in three levels: self-manage, crew medical officer review, and ground flight surgeon. It is a decision aid, not a diagnosis tool.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages and front end: TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand for state, Framer Motion for animation.
  • 3D: Three.js, with three-mesh-bvh for fast picking on the body model. Models are from Sketchfab under Creative Commons licences and need credit.
  • AI and voice: Google Gemini for speech, image review and conversation, through a small local proxy so the API key never reaches the browser. The browser’s built-in speech recognition and voice are the fallback.
  • Hardware: only a webcam and a microphone, on an ordinary laptop.
  • Reference data: spaceflight ranges informed by NASA-STD-3001.

What makes it creative

  • The reference ranges change with the habitat, and the body model’s fluid visualisation changes with gravity.
  • Vela is a conversation partner who knows your readings, not a text reader.
  • The pulse scan uses only the camera.
  • The medical brief shows how long the signal takes to reach Earth.
  • The simulator makes the whole system react live in a demo.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay. Care has to begin locally.
  • Safety. The tool does not diagnose, uses three clear tiers, and is explicit that the ranges and conditions are demo values needing flight-surgeon review.
  • Privacy. Pulse-scan video frames are processed in the browser, not uploaded. Only photos the user chooses to submit go to Gemini, and the API key stays on the local machine.
  • Reliability. Spoken lines are cached, and the browser voice takes over if Gemini fails. The rules-based checks run locally.
  • Usability. Plain language, voice or typed input, a calm dark interface, and no jargon.
  • Licensing. Third-party models are credited. One of them, the heart model, is licensed non-commercial only.

    **Note: When launching the website,give it a minute to load 3d model of human being in the self assessment page
